question: A mother brings her 8-year-old son because he wets the bed three to four nights per week. She reports he was dry at night for a period of about 8 months when he was 6, but then relapsed after starting a new school. He has no daytime wetting and no urinary symptoms. Which classification BEST describes this child's condition?

answers.text: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis — the child has never achieved sustained dryness.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary enuresis is defined as enuresis in a child who has NEVER achieved a continuous dry period of 6 months or more. This child was dry for 8 months before relapsing — he therefore has secondary enuresis, not primary.

answers.text: Secondary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis — the child relapsed after achieving at least 6 months of dryness.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Secondary (or onset) enuresis is defined as a return of bedwetting in a child who had previously been dry for at least 6 consecutive months. This child was dry for 8 months, satisfying that threshold. The 'monosymptomatic' qualifier applies because he has no daytime wetting or lower urinary tract symptoms. Secondary enuresis must always prompt a search for a precipitating cause — here, a psychosocial stressor (school change) is evident.

answers.text: Diurnal enuresis — because the onset is linked to a daytime psychosocial stressor.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diurnal (daytime) enuresis refers to involuntary wetting during waking hours. This child's wetting occurs only at night; the psychosocial stressor is a precipitant for secondary enuresis, not a criterion for daytime classification.

answers.text: Enuresis cannot be diagnosed until the child is at least 10 years old.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The diagnostic age threshold for enuresis is 5 years (for nocturnal enuresis in most guidelines). This child is 8 years old, well above the threshold. The threshold of 5 years reflects the age by which most children are expected to achieve reliable nocturnal bladder control.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the classification of enuresis. Primary enuresis = never dry for 6+ months continuously. Secondary enuresis = relapse after 6+ continuous dry months. The age threshold for diagnosis is 5 years, not 10. This 8-year-old with an 8-month dry period followed by relapse has secondary enuresis.

Correct. Secondary enuresis is defined by relapse after at least 6 continuous months of dryness. This child was dry for 8 months before the stressor-precipitated relapse, confirming secondary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis. Secondary enuresis always warrants investigation for organic and psychosocial triggers.
